claim: Language is acquired and processed in complex and dynamic naturalistic contexts, involving the simultaneous processing of connected speech, faces, bodies, objects, etc.
source: Language is acquired and processed in complex and dynamic naturalistic contexts, involving the simultaneous processing of connected speech, faces, bodies, objects, etc.
evidence: This is a general statement about language processing that draws from established understanding in cognitive science and linguistics.

claim: Across contexts, concrete and abstract concepts encode different experience-based information in separable sets of brain regions.
source: First, across contexts, concrete and abstract concepts are shown to encode different experience-based information in separable sets of brain regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental results presented in the manuscript, specifically the fMRI data analysis showing distinct brain activation patterns.

claim: The differences between concrete and abstract concept processing are reduced when multimodal context is considered.
source: However, these differences are reduced when multimodal context is considered.
evidence: This is supported by the contextual analysis results showing convergence of activation patterns.

claim: The response profile of abstract words becomes more concrete-like when these are processed in visual scenes highly related to their meaning.
source: Specifically, the response profile of abstract words becomes more concrete-like when these are processed in visual scenes highly related to their meaning.
evidence: This is supported by the situated vs. displaced context analysis showing overlap between situated abstract and concrete processing patterns.

claim: When the visual context is unrelated to a given concrete word, the activation pattern resembles more that of abstract conceptual processing.
source: Conversely, when the visual context is unrelated to a given concrete word, the activation pattern resembles more that of abstract conceptual processing.
evidence: This is supported by the displaced context analysis showing overlap between displaced concrete and abstract processing patterns.

claim: While concepts generally encode habitual experiences, the underlying neurobiological organisation is not fixed but depends dynamically on available contextual information.
source: These results suggest that while concepts generally encode habitual experiences, the underlying neurobiological organisation is not fixed but depends dynamically on available contextual information.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings showing context-dependent changes in brain activation patterns.

claim: Children may learn what the word 'tiger' means primarily via sensory-motor experience.
source: For example, children may learn what the word 'tiger' means primarily via sensory-motor experience: they see one on TV, or they are told that a tiger looks like a big cat.
evidence: This is a hypothetical example used to illustrate a concept, based on general knowledge of language acquisition.

claim: The experience required for understanding the more abstract concept of 'good' will likely include an evaluation of the rational and emotional motives underscoring intentional actions.
source: Conversely, the experience required for understanding the more abstract concept of 'good' will likely include an evaluation of the rational and emotional motives underscoring intentional actions.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about how abstract concepts are learned.

claim: Concrete concepts have external physical references (they refer to objects or actions that are easily perceived in the world).
source: Consequently, while more concrete concepts have external physical references (they refer to objects or actions that are easily perceived in the world), more abstract concepts do not necessarily have such references (they generally refer more to cultural and societal constructs or peoples' inner states of mind) (Villani et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Abstract concepts do not necessarily have external physical references and generally refer more to cultural and societal constructs or peoples' inner states of mind.
source: Consequently, while more concrete concepts have external physical references (they refer to objects or actions that are easily perceived in the world), more abstract concepts do not necessarily have such references (they generally refer more to cultural and societal constructs or peoples' inner states of mind) (Villani et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Most studies of concrete and abstract processing present words or sentences isolated from the rich contexts in which we usually process them.
source: Most studies of concrete and abstract processing are not naturalistic in that they present words or sentences isolated from the rich contexts in which we usually process them.
evidence: This is a characterization of the existing literature that can be verified by examining previous studies.

claim: Concrete and abstract concepts engage separate brain regions involved in processing different types of information.
source: Collectively, these studies suggest that concrete and abstract concepts engage separate brain regions involved in processing different types of information. (Bedny and Thompson-Schill, 2006; Binder et al., 2009; Sabsevitz et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2010; Vigliocco et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Concrete words engage regions involved in experiential processing.
source: Concrete words engage regions involved in experiential processing (Barsalou et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Motor-related cortices activate during the processing of action verbs like 'throw'.
source: For example, motor-related cortices activate during the processing of action verbs like 'throw' (Hauk et al., 2004), or action-related nouns like 'hammer' (Vigliocco et al., 2006; Kiefer and Pulvermüller, 2012), auditory cortices for sound-related words like 'telephone' (Goldberg et al., 2006; Kiefer et al., 2008), and visual cortices for color-related words like 'yellow' (Hsu et al., 2011; Simmons et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Motor-related cortices activate during the processing of action-related nouns like 'hammer'.
source: For example, motor-related cortices activate during the processing of action verbs like 'throw' (Hauk et al., 2004), or action-related nouns like 'hammer' (Vigliocco et al., 2006; Kiefer and Pulvermüller, 2012), auditory cortices for sound-related words like 'telephone' (Goldberg et al., 2006; Kiefer et al., 2008), and visual cortices for color-related words like 'yellow' (Hsu et al., 2011; Simmons et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Auditory cortices activate for sound-related words like 'telephone'.
source: For example, motor-related cortices activate during the processing of action verbs like 'throw' (Hauk et al., 2004), or action-related nouns like 'hammer' (Vigliocco et al., 2006; Kiefer and Pulvermüller, 2012), auditory cortices for sound-related words like 'telephone' (Goldberg et al., 2006; Kiefer et al., 2008), and visual cortices for color-related words like 'yellow' (Hsu et al., 2011; Simmons et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Visual cortices activate for color-related words like 'yellow'.
source: For example, motor-related cortices activate during the processing of action verbs like 'throw' (Hauk et al., 2004), or action-related nouns like 'hammer' (Vigliocco et al., 2006; Kiefer and Pulvermüller, 2012), auditory cortices for sound-related words like 'telephone' (Goldberg et al., 2006; Kiefer et al., 2008), and visual cortices for color-related words like 'yellow' (Hsu et al., 2011; Simmons et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: We learn and neurobiologically encode concrete concepts in terms of the sensory and motor experiences associated with their referents.
source: These results are consistent with the view that we learn and neurobiologically encode concrete concepts in terms of the sensory and motor experiences associated with their referents.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the cited literature and represents a theoretical position.

claim: Some studies of abstract concepts have found greater activation in brain regions associated with general linguistic processing.
source: In contrast, some studies of abstract concepts have found greater activation in brain regions associated with general linguistic processing (Binder et al., 2005; Mellet et al., 1998; Noppeney et al., 2004; Sabsevitz et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Abstract concepts are learned by understanding their role in a linguistic context, including semantic relationships with other words.
source: These findings suggest that abstract concepts are learned by understanding their role in a linguistic context, including semantic relationships with other words (e.g. 'democracy' is understood through its relationships to words like 'people,' 'parliament,' 'politics,' etc., e.g. Jones et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation of findings supported by citation.

claim: Neurobiological data support the view that subcategories of abstract concepts retain sensorimotor information.
source: However, neurobiological data also support the view that subcategories of abstract concepts retain sensorimotor information (Harpaintner et al., 2022; Harpaintner et al., 2020; Harpaintner et al., 2018; Fernandino et al., 2022) as well as social information (Villani et al., 2019; Conca et al., 2021a) and internal/interoceptive/affective experiences (Oosterwijk et al., 2015; Vigliocco et al., 2014), which are also important for learning abstract concepts (Ponari et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Subcategories of abstract concepts retain social information.
source: However, neurobiological data also support the view that subcategories of abstract concepts retain sensorimotor information (Harpaintner et al., 2022; Harpaintner et al., 2020; Harpaintner et al., 2018; Fernandino et al., 2022) as well as social information (Villani et al., 2019; Conca et al., 2021a) and internal/interoceptive/affective experiences (Oosterwijk et al., 2015; Vigliocco et al., 2014), which are also important for learning abstract concepts (Ponari et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Subcategories of abstract concepts retain internal/interoceptive/affective experiences.
source: However, neurobiological data also support the view that subcategories of abstract concepts retain sensorimotor information (Harpaintner et al., 2022; Harpaintner et al., 2020; Harpaintner et al., 2018; Fernandino et al., 2022) as well as social information (Villani et al., 2019; Conca et al., 2021a) and internal/interoceptive/affective experiences (Oosterwijk et al., 2015; Vigliocco et al., 2014), which are also important for learning abstract concepts (Ponari et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Abstract concepts constitute a more heterogeneous category.
source: Thus, abstract concepts constitute a more heterogeneous category (Roversi et al., 2013; Zdrazilova et al., 2018; Villani et al., 2019; Muraki et al., 2020; Muraki et al., 2020; Kiefer et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Previous studies have only investigated the processing of decontextualized concepts.
source: A limitation of these studies is that they have only investigated the processing of decontextualized concepts (see e.g. Table 1 in a recent review by Del Maschio et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a characterization of the literature supported by citation to a review.

claim: Previous studies often implicitly assume that conceptual representations in the brain are the product of a stable set of regions processing different types of information depending on whether a concept is concrete or abstract.
source: That is, they (often implicitly) assume that conceptual representations in the brain are the product of a stable set of regions processing different types of information depending on whether a concept is concrete or abstract.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the assumptions underlying previous research.

claim: The information encoded during conceptual processing depends on the contextual information available.
source: However, this dichotomy may not account for the way in which we typically process concepts (Lebois et al., 2015), given that the information encoded during conceptual processing depends on the contextual information available.
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents a theoretical position.

claim: The situated processing of concrete concepts like 'chair' could be linked to many abstract internal elements like goals, motivations, emotions, and theory of mind.
source: For example, the situated (i.e. contextualized in the discourse but also in the physical setting in which processing occurs) processing of concrete concepts like 'chair' could be linked to many abstract internal elements like goals ('I want to rest'), motivations ('I have been standing for 2 hr'), emotions ('I would like to feel comfortable'), and theory of mind ('is that older person more in the need of this chair than me?').
evidence: This is a hypothetical example used to illustrate how context affects conceptual processing.

claim: An abstract concept like 'truth' is no longer particularly abstract when used in reference to a perceived physical situation that matches the utterance's meaning.
source: Conversely, an abstract concept like 'truth' is no longer particularly abstract when used in reference to a perceived physical situation (such as 'snowing') that matches the utterance's meaning ('it is true that it is snowing'). Here, 'truth' refers to a concrete state of the world (Barsalou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a hypothetical example supported by citation.

claim: Previous work has postulated flexible conceptual processing in experiential brain circuits.
source: Indeed, previous work has postulated flexible conceptual processing in experiential brain circuits (Binder and Desai, 2011; Pulvermüller, 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Behavioral data support the view that contextual information can affect conceptual processing.
source: Behavioral data support the view that contextual information can affect conceptual processing (e.g., Chambers et al., 2004; Cooper, 1974; Tanenhaus et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous behavioral studies.

claim: When an object is depicted in a visual context consistent with its use, the action associated with using the object is more readily available than when the context is more consistent with picking the object up.
source: For example, when an object is depicted in a visual context consistent with its use, the action associated with using the object is more readily available than when the context is more consistent with picking the object up (Kalénine et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: There is neurobiological evidence that objects visually present in a situation can influence conceptual processing.
source: There is also neurobiological evidence that objects visually present in a situation can influence conceptual processing (Hoffman et al., 2013; Yee and Thompson-Schill, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous neuroimaging studies.

claim: Task-related color-congruency of objects correlates with less activation of brain regions involved in color perception during processing.
source: For example, task-related color-congruency of objects correlates with less activation of brain regions involved in color perception during processing – likely because less retrieval of detailed color knowledge was necessary (Hsu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Dynamic, context-dependent recruitment of visual and motor-related areas during semantic processing has been established.
source: Dynamic, context-dependent recruitment of visual and motor-related areas during semantic processing has also been established (Hoenig et al., 2008; van Dam et al., 2012; Popp et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: An understanding of conceptual knowledge as static and context-independent is insufficient to account for the dynamics of semantic processing.
source: An understanding of conceptual knowledge as static and context-independent is insufficient to account for these dynamics (Pulvermüller, 2018b).
evidence: This is a theoretical position supported by citation.

claim: No previous study has addressed whether the brain areas associated with concrete and abstract concepts are fixed or recruited in a more dynamic way during semantic processing.
source: However, no previous study has addressed whether the brain areas associated with concrete and abstract concepts are fixed or recruited in a more dynamic way during semantic processing.
evidence: This is a characterization of the gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: Results from previous investigations of conceptual processing reflect the average experiential information of the type of situational context in which concepts are habitually experienced.
source: First, we submit that results from previous investigations of conceptual processing, which generally depict a stable dichotomy between concrete and abstract words, reflect the average experiential information of the type of situational context in which concepts are habitually experienced.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction made by the authors.

claim: The neurobiological representation of concrete concepts will be related to associated brain regions because they retain experiences related to their physical referents that are predominantly characterized by sensory and motor information.
source: Therefore, we predict that the neurobiological representation of concrete concepts, will be related to associated brain regions, because they retain experiences related to their physical referents that are predominantly characterized by sensory and motor information, (Pulvermüller, 2018b; Willems et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a prediction made by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: Abstract concepts are expected to activate brain regions associated with emotional, interoceptive, and general linguistic processing.
source: In contrast, because their representations mostly reflect information related to internal/interoceptive/affective experience as well as linguistic information, we expect abstract concepts to activate brain regions associated with emotional, interoceptive, and general linguistic processing (Reinboth and Farkaš, 2022).
evidence: This is a prediction made by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: Habitual representations of concepts are not necessarily stable and might change during naturalistic processing depending on the specific contextual information available.
source: Second, the reviewed work also suggests that these habitual representations are not necessarily stable and might change during naturalistic processing depending on the specific contextual information available.
evidence: This is a prediction based on review of previous literature.

claim: A concept is displaced if its context offers little or no visual information related to the concept's external sensory-motor features.
source: We specify two context conditions: a concept is displaced if its context offers little or no visual information related to the concept's external sensory-motor features.
evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors for their experimental design.

claim: A concept is situated if its visual context contains objects related to its meaning.
source: In contrast, a concept is situated, if its visual context contains objects related to its meaning.
evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors for their experimental design.

claim: When a concrete concept is processed in displaced situations, response profiles will shift towards more internalized processing shared with abstract concepts.
source: We predict that when a concrete concept is processed in displaced situations (e.g. 'cat' processed when discussing the general character traits of cats vs dogs), response profiles will shift towards more internalized processing shared with abstract concepts.
evidence: This is a prediction made by the authors.

claim: When an abstract concept is processed in a situated context, its representation will more heavily draw on regions involved in processing external, visual information that otherwise characterize more concrete concepts.
source: In contrast, when an abstract concept is processed in a situated context (for example the word 'love' processed in a scene with people kissing), its representation will more heavily draw on regions involved in processing external, visual information that otherwise characterize more concrete concepts.
evidence: This is a prediction made by the authors.

claim: Both concrete and abstract concepts draw on information related to experience (external and internal) as well as linguistic association.
source: We propose that this erosion of the concrete/abstract dichotomy for contextualized processing shows that both concrete and abstract concepts draw on information related to experience (external and internal) as well as linguistic association.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation proposed by the authors.

claim: Which neurobiological structures are engaged during conceptual processing depends dynamically on the contextual information available.
source: Which associated neurobiological structures are engaged during processing depends dynamically on the contextual information available.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation proposed by the authors.

claim: Concrete produced more modulation than abstract processing in parts of the frontal lobes, including the right posterior inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) and the precentral sulcus.
source: This showed that concrete produced more modulation than abstract processing in parts of the frontal lobes, including the right posterior inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) and the precentral sulcus (Figure 1, red).
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data analysis results shown in Figure 1.

claim: The IFG has been hypothesized to be involved in the processing of action-related words and sentences, supporting both semantic decision tasks and the retrieval of lexical semantic information.
source: Known for its role in language processing and semantic retrieval, the IFG has been hypothesized to be involved in the processing of action-related words and sentences, supporting both semantic decision tasks and the retrieval of lexical semantic information (Bookheimer, 2002; Hagoort, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The precentral sulcus is linked to the processing of action verbs and motor-related words.
source: The precentral sulcus is similarly linked to the processing of action verbs and motor-related words (Pulvermüller, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Greater modulation for concrete words occurred in the bilateral transverse temporal gyrus and sulcus, planum polare, and temporale.
source: In the temporal lobes, greater modulation occurred in the bilateral transverse temporal gyrus and sulcus, planum polare, and temporale.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data analysis results.

claim: Primary and secondary auditory cortices are crucial for phonological and auditory processing, with implications for the processing of sound-related words and environmental sounds.
source: These areas, including primary and secondary auditory cortices, are crucial for phonological and auditory processing, with implications for the processing of sound-related words and environmental sounds (Binder and Desai, 2011) .
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The superior temporal gyrus (STG) and sulcus (STS) showed greater modulation for concrete words.
source: The superior temporal gyrus (STG) and sulcus (STS) also showed greater modulation for concrete words and these are said to be central to auditory processing and the integration of phonological, syntactic, and semantic information, with a particular role in processing meaningful speech and narratives (Hickok and Poeppel, 2007) .
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data analysis results and citation.

claim: The STG and STS are central to auditory processing and the integration of phonological, syntactic, and semantic information, with a particular role in processing meaningful speech and narratives.
source: The superior temporal gyrus (STG) and sulcus (STS) also showed greater modulation for concrete words and these are said to be central to auditory processing and the integration of phonological, syntactic, and semantic information, with a particular role in processing meaningful speech and narratives (Hickok and Poeppel, 2007) .
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: More concrete modulated activity was found bilaterally in the precuneus.
source: In the parietal and occipital lobes, more concrete modulated activity was found bilaterally in the precuneus, which has been associated with visuospatial imagery, episodic memory retrieval, and self-processing operations and has been said to contribute to the visualization aspects of concrete concepts (Cavanna and Trimble, 2006) .
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data analysis results and citation.

claim: The precuneus has been associated with visuospatial imagery, episodic memory retrieval, and self-processing operations and has been said to contribute to the visualization aspects of concrete concepts.
source: In the parietal and occipital lobes, more concrete modulated activity was found bilaterally in the precuneus, which has been associated with visuospatial imagery, episodic memory retrieval, and self-processing operations and has been said to contribute to the visualization aspects of concrete concepts (Cavanna and Trimble, 2006) .
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: More activation for concrete words was found in large swaths of the occipital cortices and the ventral visual stream.
source: More activation was also found in large swaths of the occipital cortices (running into the inferior temporal lobe), and the ventral visual stream.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data analysis results.

claim: The ventral visual stream is integral to visual processing, with the ventral stream particularly involved in object recognition and categorization.
source: These regions are integral to visual processing, with the ventral stream (including areas like the fusiform gyrus) particularly involved in object recognition and categorization, linking directly to the visual representation of concrete concepts (Simmons et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The dorsal and posterior medial cerebellum were more active bilaterally for concrete modulation.
source: Finally, subcortically, the dorsal and posterior medial cerebellum were more active bilaterally for concrete modulation.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data analysis results.

claim: Some studies implicate the cerebellum in cognitive and linguistic processing, including the modulation of language and semantic processing through its connections with cerebral cortical areas.
source: Traditionally associated with motor function, some studies also implicate the cerebellum in cognitive and linguistic processing, including the modulation of language and semantic processing through its connections with cerebral cortical areas (Stoodley and Schmahmann, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Activation for abstract was greater than concrete words in the right anterior cingulate gyrus, lateral and medial aspects of the superior frontal gyrus.
source: Conversely, activation for abstract was greater than concrete words in the following regions (Figure 1, blue): In the frontal lobes, this included the right anterior cingulate gyrus, lateral and medial aspects of the superior frontal gyrus.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data analysis results shown in Figure 1.

claim: The anterior cingulate gyrus and superior frontal gyrus are involved in cognitive control, decision-making, and emotional processing and may contribute to abstract conceptualization by integrating affective and cognitive components.
source: Being involved in cognitive control, decision-making, and emotional processing, these areas may contribute to abstract conceptualization by integrating affective and cognitive components (Shenhav et al., 2013) .
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citation.

claim: More left frontal activity for abstract words was found in both lateral and medial prefrontal cortices, and in the orbital gyrus.
source: More left frontal activity was found in both lateral and medial prefrontal cortices, and in the orbital gyrus, regions which are key to social cognition, valuation, and decision-making, all domains rich in abstract concepts (Amodio and Frith, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data analysis results and citation.

claim: Lateral and medial prefrontal cortices and the orbital gyrus are key to social cognition, valuation, and decision-making, all domains rich in abstract concepts.
source: More left frontal activity was found in both lateral and medial prefrontal cortices, and in the orbital gyrus, regions which are key to social cognition, valuation, and decision-making, all domains rich in abstract concepts (Amodio and Frith, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Bilateral activity for abstract words was greater in the angular gyri (AG) and inferior parietal lobules, including the postcentral gyrus.
source: In the parietal lobes, bilateral activity was greater in the angular gyri (AG) and inferior parietal lobules, including the postcentral gyrus.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data analysis results.

claim: The angular gyri and inferior parietal lobules are central to the default mode network and are implicated in semantic processing, abstract thinking, and integrating sensory information with autobiographical memory.
source: Central to the default mode network, these regions are implicated in a wide range of complex cognitive functions, including semantic processing, abstract thinking, and integrating sensory information with autobiographical memory (Seghier, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Activity for abstract words was restricted to the STS bilaterally in the temporal lobes.
source: In the temporal lobes, activity was restricted to the STS bilaterally, which plays a critical role in the perception of intentionality and social interactions, essential for understanding abstract social concepts (Frith and Frith, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data analysis results and citation.

claim: The STS plays a critical role in the perception of intentionality and social interactions, essential for understanding abstract social concepts.
source: In the temporal lobes, activity was restricted to the STS bilaterally, which plays a critical role in the perception of intentionality and social interactions, essential for understanding abstract social concepts (Frith and Frith, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Activity for abstract words was greater bilaterally in the anterior thalamus, nucleus accumbens, and left amygdala.
source: Subcortically, activity was greater, bilaterally, in the anterior thalamus, nucleus accumbens, and left amygdala for abstract modulation.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data analysis results.

claim: The anterior thalamus, nucleus accumbens, and amygdala are involved in motivation, reward processing, and the integration of emotional information with memory, relevant for abstract concepts related to emotions and social relations.
source: These areas are involved in motivation, reward processing, and the integration of emotional information with memory, relevant for abstract concepts related to emotions and social relations (Haber and Knutson, 2010; Phelps and LeDoux, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There was an overlap in activity between modulation of both concreteness and abstractness in the left IFG, AG, and STG.
source: Finally, there was an overlap in activity between modulation of both concreteness and abstractness (Figure 1, yellow). The overlap activity is due to the fact that we performed general linear tests for the abstract/concrete contrast at each of the 20 timepoints in our group analysis. Consequently, overlap means that activation in these regions is modulated by both concrete and abstract word processing but at different time-scales. In particular, we find that activity modulation associated with abstractness is generally processed over a longer time-frame (for a comparison of significant timing differences see Figure 1—figure supplement 2). In the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes, this was primarily in the left IFG, AG, and STG, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data analysis results shown in Figure 1.

claim: Overlap in activity means that activation in these regions is modulated by both concrete and abstract word processing but at different time-scales.
source: The overlap activity is due to the fact that we performed general linear tests for the abstract/concrete contrast at each of the 20 timepoints in our group analysis. Consequently, overlap means that activation in these regions is modulated by both concrete and abstract word processing but at different time-scales.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the analysis method and results.

claim: Activity modulation associated with abstractness is generally processed over a longer time-frame.
source: In particular, we find that activity modulation associated with abstractness is generally processed over a longer time-frame (for a comparison of significant timing differences see Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the timing analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Left IFG is prominently involved in semantic processing, particularly in tasks requiring semantic selection and retrieval.
source: Left IFG is prominently involved in semantic processing, particularly in tasks requiring semantic selection and retrieval, and has been shown to play a critical role in accessing semantic memory and resolving semantic ambiguities, processes that are inherently time-consuming and reflective of the extended processing time for abstract concepts (Thompson-Schill et al., 1999; Wagner et al., 2001; Hoffman et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The STG is critical for the comprehension of complex linguistic structures, including narrative and discourse processing.
source: The STG, particularly its posterior portion, is critical for the comprehension of complex linguistic structures, including narrative and discourse processing. The processing of abstract concepts often necessitates the integration of contextual cues and inferential processing, tasks that engage the STG and may extend the temporal dynamics of semantic processing (Ferstl et al., 2008; Vandenberghe et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Processing of concrete and abstract words overlapped bilaterally around the calcarine sulcus in the occipital lobe.
source: In the occipital lobe, processing overlapped bilaterally around the calcarine sulcus, which is associated with primary visual processing (Kanwisher et al., 1997; Kosslyn et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data analysis results and citations.

claim: The calcarine sulcus is associated with primary visual processing.
source: In the occipital lobe, processing overlapped bilaterally around the calcarine sulcus, which is associated with primary visual processing (Kanwisher et al., 1997; Kosslyn et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Significantly more concrete clusters are related to the term 'Movement' compared to abstract clusters (H(2) = 12.4, p<0.001).
source: Term-based labeling demonstrates that significantly more concrete clusters are related to the term 'Movement' compared to abstract clusters (H(2) = 12.4, p<0.001; Figure 2, red).
evidence: This is supported by the meta-analytic results shown in Figure 2.

claim: Abstract clusters are more related to terms associated with internal/interoceptive/affective processing compared to concrete activation clusters, including 'Autobiographical Memory,' 'Nausea,' 'Pain,' 'Reward/Motivation,' and 'Valence' (all ps <0.05).
source: In contrast, abstract clusters are more related to terms that are arguably associated with internal/interoceptive/affective processing compared to concrete activation clusters, i.e., 'Autobiographical Memory,' 'Nausea,' 'Pain,' 'Reward/Motivation,' and 'Valence' (all ps <0.05; Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by the meta-analytic results shown in Figure 2.

claim: 'Language' was the only term more associated with overlapping clusters than either concrete (H(2) = 7, p<0.001) or abstract clusters (H(2) = 4, p=0.045).
source: Finally, 'Language' was the only term more associated with overlapping clusters than either concrete (H(2) = 7, p<0.001) or abstract clusters (H(2) = 4, p=0.045; Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by the meta-analytic results shown in Figure 2.

claim: There were significantly more concrete compared to abstract clusters associated with the dimension 'Torso' (H(2)=7, p<0.001).
source: Comparing dimensions for abstract vs concrete modulated clusters, we found significantly more concrete compared to abstract clusters associated with the dimension 'Torso' H(2)=7, p<0.001.
evidence: This is supported by the peaks and valleys analysis results shown in Figure 3.

claim: Three concrete clusters were associated with 'Haptic' and 'Mouth,' which was significantly more than for abstract clusters (all tests H(2)=5.2, all p's = 0.02).
source: Three concrete clusters were associated with 'Haptic' and 'Mouth,' which was also significantly more than for abstract clusters (all tests H(2)=5.2, all p's = 0.02).
evidence: This is supported by the peaks and valleys analysis results.

claim: Eight abstract clusters were significantly more associated with the dimension 'Valence' than concrete clusters (H(2)=8.3, p<0.001).
source: Conversely, eight abstract clusters were significantly more associated with the dimension 'Valence' than concrete clusters (H(2)=8.3, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by the peaks and valleys analysis results shown in Figure 3.

claim: Five clusters in which modulation through concreteness and abstractness overlapped were significantly more associated with the dimension 'Mouth' compared to two concrete clusters (H(2) = 5.1, p=0.03) and 0 abstract clusters (H(2)=7.8, p<0.001).
source: Finally, five clusters in which modulation through concreteness and abstractness overlapped (though at different time points) were significantly more associated with the dimension 'Mouth' compared to two concrete clusters H(2) = 5.1, p=0.03 and 0 abstract clusters H(2)=7.8, p<0.001.
evidence: This is supported by the peaks and valleys analysis results shown in Figure 3.

claim: Concrete words were associated with multiple regions involved in sensory and motor processing.
source: Indeed, we found a general tendency for concrete and abstract words to activate regions associated with different experiences (Figure 1). Consistent with prior work, concrete words were associated with multiple regions involved in sensory and motor processing (Mkrtychian et al., 2019), including most of the visual system (Gao et al., 2019) and the right frontal motor system (Pulvermüller, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI results and citations to previous research.

claim: Abstract words engaged regions typically associated with internal/interoceptive/affective processing.
source: In contrast, abstract words engaged regions typically associated with internal/interoceptive/affective processing (anterior thalamus, somatosensory cortex)(Harpaintner et al., 2018; Villani et al., 2021), autobiographical memory (anterior medial prefrontal regions) (Conca et al., 2021a), and emotional processing and regulation (anterior medial prefrontal regions, orbital prefrontal cortex, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, nucleus accumbens and amygdala) (Vigliocco et al., 2014; Conca et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI results and citations to previous research.

claim: Meta-analytic and peak and valley analyses showed that concrete regions were more associated with sensory-motor properties whereas abstract regions were more associated with internal/interoceptive/affective properties.
source: Consistent with this, both meta-analytic and peak and valley analyses showed that concrete regions were more associated with sensory-motor properties (e.g. 'Movement' and 'Hand_Arm') whereas abstract regions were more associated with internal/interoceptive/affective properties (e.g. 'Valence;' Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by the meta-analytic and peaks and valleys analysis results shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: These results provide evidence from naturalistic processing that concrete and abstract concepts encode different types of experiences.
source: Together, these results provide evidence from naturalistic processing that concrete and abstract concepts encode different types of experiences (Vigliocco et al., 2009; Barsalou and Wiemer-Hastings, 2005; Kiehl et al., 1999).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results supported by citations.

claim: The study's results show greater activation for concrete words in temporo-parieto-occipital regions.
source: At the level of brain regions, our study aligns with previous literature identifying distinct brain regions engaged in processing abstract versus concrete words. Specifically, our results show greater activation for concrete words in temporo-parieto-occipital regions.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data analysis results.

claim: Abstract word processing preferentially engages a network of regions within the left hemisphere, including the inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), superior and middle temporal gyri, and the inferior parietal lobule.
source: Conversely, our study found that abstract word processing preferentially engages a network of regions within the left hemisphere, including the inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), superior and middle temporal gyri, and the inferior parietal lobule.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data analysis results.

claim: Regions involved in sensory and motor processing are involved in processing both concrete and abstract words.
source: However, the regions involved in processing concrete and abstract concepts across contexts did not imply a fully dichotomous encoding of experiences. First, we found that regions involved in sensory (mostly in visual cortices) and motor processing are involved in processing both types of words (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data analysis results shown in Figure 1.

claim: There was overlap activation in regions associated with language processing in general.
source: Moreover, we found overlap activation in regions associated with language processing in general (Tang et al., 2022, Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data analysis results and citation.

claim: Such results are in line with proposals in which both concrete and abstract representations rely on experiential information as well as their linguistic relationships with other words.
source: Such results are in line with proposals in which both concrete and abstract representations rely on experiential information as well as their linguistic relationships with other words (e.g. Vigliocco et al., 2009; Vigliocco et al., 2009; Piantadosi and Hill, 2022).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Information related to 'Mouth' drives activation in overlap clusters.
source: This latter hypothesis is also supported by our Peaks and Valleys analysis, more specifically that information related to 'Mouth' (i.e. the language organ) drives activation in overlap clusters.
evidence: This is supported by the peaks and valleys analysis results.

claim: This is evidence against hypotheses in which the mouth is specifically associated with abstract concepts.
source: This is furthermore evidence against hypotheses in which the mouth is specifically associated with abstract concepts (Borghi and Zarcone, 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in relation to a specific hypothesis from previous work.

claim: Brain activation underlying concrete and abstract conceptual processing fundamentally changes as a function of visual context.
source: We find that brain activation underlying concrete and abstract conceptual processing fundamentally changes as a function of visual context.
evidence: This is supported by the contextual analysis results.

claim: Concrete concepts become more abstract-like in displaced contexts with less relevant visual information.
source: Our results show that concrete concepts become more abstract-like in displaced contexts with less relevant visual information (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by the contextual analysis results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Overlap between activation for concrete concepts in displaced conditions and abstract concepts across context can be found in ACC, thalamus, and large swaths of the anterior, middle, and posterior temporal lobe.
source: Overlap between activation for concrete concepts in displaced conditions and abstract concepts across context (Figure 5A) can be found in ACC, thalamus, and large swaths of the anterior, middle, and posterior temporal lobe.
evidence: This is supported by the spatial correlation analysis results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: When a concrete concept is processed in a displaced context, its representation will relate more to internal/interoceptive variables and linguistic associations, which are usually encoded by abstract concepts.
source: We propose that this is because, when a concrete concept is processed in a displaced context, its representation will relate more to internal/interoceptive variables and linguistic associations, which are usually encoded by abstract concepts.
evidence: This is an interpretation proposed by the authors based on the data.

claim: Abstract concepts become more concrete-like when they are highly situated.
source: Conversely, abstract concepts become more concrete-like when they are highly situated (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the contextual analysis results shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Overlap between activation for abstract concepts in situated conditions and concrete concepts across context can be found in fusiform and the occipital lobe (bilateral).
source: Overlap between activation for abstract concepts in situated conditions and concrete concepts across context (Figure 5B) can be found in fusiform and the occipital lobe (bilateral).
evidence: This is supported by the spatial correlation analysis results shown in Figure 5B.

claim: An abstract concept processed in a situated context relates more to external visual information, which is usually encoded by concrete concepts.
source: We propose that this is because an abstract concept processed in a situated context relates more to external visual information, which is usually encoded by concrete concepts.
evidence: This is an interpretation proposed by the authors based on the data.

claim: The concrete/abstract distinction is neurobiologically less stable than might be assumed.
source: A consequence of this finding is that the concrete/abstract distinction is neurobiologically less stable than might be assumed.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Brain regions 'switch alliance' during concrete or abstract word processing depending on context.
source: Brain regions 'switch alliance' during concrete or abstract word processing depending on context.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Variance in visual context interacted with word-type in regions commonly defined as the DMN, as well as a set of prefrontal regions associated with semantic control.
source: Our results indicate that variance in visual context interacted with word-type (both concrete and abstract) in regions commonly defined as the DMN, as well as a set of prefrontal regions associated with semantic control (Ralph et al., 2017; Hoffman et al., 2018; Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by the interaction analysis results and citations.

claim: Recent literature on the role of the DMN suggests that these regions reactivate memories and contexts-specific information.
source: Recent literature on the role of the DMN suggests that these regions reactivate memories (Crittenden et al., 2015; Konishi et al., 2015; Murphy et al., 2018; Sormaz et al., 2018; Yee and Thompson-Schill, 2016; Andrews-Hanna et al., 2014, Vatansever et al., 2017) and contexts-specific information (Hahamy et al., 2023), possibly to form contextually relevant situation models (Chen et al., 2015; Raykov et al., 2020, Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012, Smith et al., 2021, Smith et al., 2017), in order to guide semantic cognition (Binder et al., 1999; Fernandino et al., 2016; Yeshurun et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent literature.

claim: The DMN is especially involved in displaced conditions for both concrete and abstract conceptual processing.
source: Breaking up the interaction between word_type and context, we find that the DMN is especially involved in displaced conditions for both concrete and abstract conceptual processing (see Figure 4A, B (blue)).
evidence: This is supported by the interaction analysis results shown in Figure 4.

claim: These results fit well with evidence suggesting that the DMN supports conceptual processing especially when displaced from sensorimotor input.
source: These results fit well with evidence suggesting that the DMN supports conceptual processing especially when displaced from sensorimotor input (Murphy et al., 2018; Lanzoni et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The DMN is most strongly activated in the displaced conditions involving abstract concepts.
source: Accordingly, the DMN is most strongly activated in the displaced conditions involving abstract concepts.
evidence: This is supported by the interaction analysis results.

claim: Given their inherent lack of sensorimotor information, abstract concepts offer a greater degree of displacement than their concrete counterparts, thereby demanding a higher engagement of the DMN in these conditions.
source: Given their inherent lack of sensorimotor information, abstract concepts offer a greater degree of displacement than their concrete counterparts, thereby demanding a higher engagement of the DMN in these conditions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results.

claim: The mechanisms observed may extend beyond visual processing to encompass more general sensory processing mechanisms.
source: In considering the impact of visual context on the neural encoding of concepts generally, it is furthermore essential to recognize that the mechanisms observed may extend beyond visual processing to encompass more general sensory processing mechanisms.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the generalizability of the findings.

claim: The human brain is adept at integrating information across sensory modalities to form coherent conceptual representations.
source: The human brain is adept at integrating information across sensory modalities to form coherent conceptual representations, a process that is critical for navigating the multimodal nature of real-world experiences (Barsalou et al., 2018; Smith, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and represents established knowledge.

claim: Similar effects to those observed with visual context may be observed in contexts that engage other sensory modalities.
source: While our findings highlight the role of visual context in modulating the neural representation of abstract and concrete words, similar effects may be observed in contexts that engage other sensory modalities.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future findings.

claim: The exact relationship between concepts and language remains an open question.
source: The exact relationship between concepts and language remains an open question, but it is undisputed that, as determinants of meaning, concepts are necessary for language (Jackendoff, 2002; Bloom, 2000; Fauconnier and Turner, 2002).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The present study examined language-driven conceptual processing by looking at brain activation during word processing.
source: The present study examined language-driven conceptual processing, as we looked at brain activation during word processing.
evidence: This is a description of what the study did.

claim: The underlying neurobiological processes of language-driven conceptual processing are dynamically distributed and contextually determined.
source: Our results imply that the underlying neurobiological processes are dynamically distributed and contextually determined.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's results.

claim: This view fits well with models of 'natural' organization of language in the brain where language processing is a whole brain process whose patterns of activation are determined by available context.
source: This view fits well with models of 'natural' organization of language in the brain where it is argued that language processing more generally is a whole brain process whose patterns of activation are determined by available context (Skipper and Willems, 2015; Skipper and Willems, 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: More distributed regions may be averaged away when indiscriminately analyzed together and following thresholding because they are more variable given they are associated with different experiences, linguistic categories, and processes.
source: These more distributed regions may be averaged away when indiscriminately analyzed together and following thresholding because (i) they are more variable given they are associated with different experiences (as we have seen here), linguistic categories (e.g. 'formulaic speech;' see Skipper et al., 2022), and processes (e.g. different types of syntax) (ii) there are individual differences in all of these (e.g. Skipper et al., 2022; Skipper and Willems, 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Concrete and abstract modulation overlaps in typical perisylvian 'language regions'.
source: These suppositions are supported by the fact that concrete and abstract modulation overlaps in typical perisylvian 'language regions' (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The study analyzed the 'Naturalistic Neuroimaging Database (NNDb)'.
source: The present study analyzed the 'Naturalistic Neuroimaging Database (NNDb)' (Aliko et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a description of the data source used in the study.

claim: The Naturalistic Neuroimaging Database includes 86 right-handed participants (42 females, range of age 18–58 years, M = 26.81, SD = 10.09 years) undergoing fMRI while watching one of 10 full-length movies.
source: The Naturalistic Neuroimaging Database (Aliko et al., 2020, https://openneuro.org/datasets/ds002837/versions/2.0.0) includes 86 right-handed participants (42 females, range of age 18–58 years, M = 26.81, SD = 10.09 years) undergoing fMRI while watching one of 10 full-length movies selected across a range of genres.
evidence: This is a description of the dataset used in the study.

claim: All participants had unimpaired hearing and (corrected) vision.
source: All had unimpaired hearing and (corrected) vision.
evidence: This is a description of participant characteristics.

claim: None of the participants had any contraindication for magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), history of psychiatric or neurological disorder, or language-related learning disabilities.
source: None had any contraindication for magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), history of psychiatric or neurological disorder, or language-related learning disabilities.
evidence: This is a description of participant exclusion criteria.

claim: All participants gave informed consent, and the study was approved by the University College London Ethics Committee (Reference Number 143/003).
source: All participants gave informed consent, and the study was approved by the University College London Ethics Committee (Reference Number 143/003).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: Functional and anatomical images were obtained using a 1.5T Siemens MAGNETOM Avanto, equipped with a 32-channel head coil.
source: Functional and anatomical images were obtained using a 1.5T Siemens MAGNETOM Avanto, equipped with a 32-channel head coil.
evidence: This is a description of the MRI equipment used.

claim: Whole-brain images were captured, each consisting of 40 slices per volume at an isotropic resolution of 3.2 mm.
source: Whole-brain images were captured, each consisting of 40 slices per volume at an isotropic resolution of 3.2 mm.
evidence: This is a description of the imaging parameters.

claim: Images were obtained using a multiband echo-planar imaging (EPI) sequence with no in-plane acceleration, a multiband factor of 4 x, a repetition time of 1 s, an echo time of 54.8 milliseconds, and a flip angle of 75 degrees.
source: These were obtained using a multiband echo-planar imaging (EPI) sequence with no in-plane acceleration, a multiband factor of 4 x, a repetition time of 1 s, an echo time of 54.8 milliseconds, and a flip angle of 75 degrees.
evidence: This is a description of the imaging sequence parameters.

claim: The data were preprocessed with AFNI and included despiking, slice-time correction, coregistration, blurring, and nonlinear alignment to the MNI152 template brain.
source: The data were preprocessed with AFNI (Cox, 1996) and included despiking, slice-time correction, coregistration, blurring, and nonlinear alignment to the MNI152 template brain.
evidence: This is a description of the preprocessing steps.

claim: All words in the movies were annotated using automated approaches with a machine learning-based speech-to-text transcription tool from Amazon Web Services (AWS).
source: All words in the movies were annotated using automated approaches with a machine learning-based speech-to-text transcription tool from Amazon Web Services (AWS; https://aws.amazon.com/transcribe/).
evidence: This is a description of the annotation method.

claim: Concrete and abstract words were selected from existing Warriner et al., 2013 norms.
source: Concrete and abstract words were selected for the present study from existing Warriner et al., 2013 norms.
evidence: This is a description of the word selection method.

claim: In the Warriner et al., 2013 database, 37,058 words were rated for concreteness on a scale from 0 (not experience-based) to 5 (experience-based) by over 4000 participants.
source: In this database, 37,058 words were rated for concreteness on a scale from 0 (not experience-based) to 5 (experience-based) by over 4000 participants.
evidence: This is a description of the norms database used.

claim: Words were median split on the concreteness scale to yield the set of concrete and abstract words.
source: We median split only content words on this scale to yield our set of concrete and abstract words.
evidence: This is a description of the word selection method.

claim: Concrete and abstract words were matched for word frequency within 1 SD of mean log frequency (3.61), using the SUTBLEX (US) corpus.
source: These were matched for word frequency within 1 SD of mean log frequency (3.61), using the SUTBLEX (US) corpus Brysbaert and New, 2009, which contains frequency counts for 72,286 words.
evidence: This is a description of the word matching procedure.

claim: Concrete and abstract words were matched to be within 1SD from mean length measured as number of letters (4.81).
source: Concrete and abstract words were also matched to be within 1SD from mean length measured as number of letters (4.81).
evidence: This is a description of the word matching procedure.

claim: After the matching process, there were 783 concrete words and 440 abstract words on average per movie.
source: After this matching process, we were left with more concrete words than abstract words in all movies (783 on average for concrete words; 440 for abstract words).
evidence: This is a description of the word counts after matching.

claim: A subset of 440 concrete words was randomly selected in each movie to match the amount of abstract words.
source: To maintain equal numbers in the subsequent analysis, we randomly selected a subset of 440 concrete words in each movie to match the amount of abstract words, leaving us with 880 words (half concrete, half abstract) per movie on average.
evidence: This is a description of the word selection procedure.

claim: Mean concreteness rating for the resulting set of concrete words was 3.22, compared to 1.83 for abstract words.
source: Mean concreteness rating for the resulting set of concrete words was 3.22, compared to 1.83 for abstract words.
evidence: This is a description of the word characteristics.

claim: The final mean log frequency and mean length for the final set of concrete words was 3.69 and 4.91 compared to 3.46 and 5.27 for the final set of abstract words and were not significantly different as determined by t-tests (all p's>0.45).
source: The final mean log frequency and mean length for the final set of concrete words was 3.69 and 4.91 compared to 3.46 and 5.27 for the final set of abstract words and were not significantly different as determined by t-tests (all p's>0.45).
evidence: This is a description of the word matching results.

claim: Surprisal given preceding linguistic context was extracted with a customized script making use of the predictive processing nature of GPT-2.
source: Surprisal given preceding linguistic context (within the same time window) was extracted with a customized script making use of the predictive processing nature of GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019), which has been shown to be a good model of processing difficulty (Wilcox et al., 2021; Duan et al., 2020; Merkx and Frank, 2021; Schrimpf et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a description of the surprisal extraction method, supported by citations.

claim: Mean surprisal of concrete words was 22.19 bits, mean surprisal of abstract words was 21.86 bits, and this difference was not significant (t=1.23, p=0.218).
source: Mean surprisal of concrete words was 22.19 bits, mean surprisal of abstract words was 21.86 bits. A t-test revealed that this difference was not significant (t=1.23, p=0.218).
evidence: This is a description of the surprisal analysis results.

claim: Mean semantic diversity of concrete words was 1.92 and 1.96 of abstract words, and this difference was not significant (t=−1.20, p=0.230).
source: Mean semantic diversity of concrete words was 1.92 and 1.96 of abstract words. This difference was also not significant (t=−1.20, p=0.230).
evidence: This is a description of the semantic diversity analysis results.

claim: Luminance and loudness for each frame in the movie was measured using the 'Librosa' package for music and audio analysis in Python.
source: We used luminance and loudness to control for visual and acoustic properties of the movies that might vary more or less for concrete or abstract words. These 'low-level' features might be correlated with other potentially confounding auditory and visual variables. For example, luminance correlates significantly with stimulus intensity and contrast (Johnson and Casson, 1995) and loudness correlates with pitch (Wengenroth et al., 2014), prosody (Couper-Kuhlen, 2004), and speaking rate (Kuhlmann et al., 2022). Thus, luminance and loudness for each frame in the movie was measured using the 'Librosa' package for music and audio analysis in Python (McFee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the method for measuring luminance and loudness, supported by citations.

claim: Mean luminance for concrete words was 0.72, compared to 0.65 for abstract words, and these were significantly different (t(4798)=9.13 p<0.001).
source: Mean luminance for concrete words was 0.72, compared to 0.65 for abstract words. These were significantly different (t(4798)=9.13 p<0.001).
evidence: This is a description of the luminance analysis results.

claim: The mean loudness for concrete words was 0.69, compared to 0.77 for abstract words, and these were significantly different (t(4798)=9.86, p<0.001).
source: The mean loudness for concrete words was 0.69, compared to 0.77 for abstract words. These were also significantly different (t(4798)=9.86, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a description of the loudness analysis results.

claim: An amplitude modulated deconvolution regression was used to estimate activity associated with concrete and abstract words from the preprocessed fMRI data.
source: We used an amplitude (also known as parametric) modulated deconvolution regression to estimate activity associated with concrete and abstract words from the preprocessed fMRI data.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method.

claim: In contrast to a standard convolution-based regression analysis, deconvolution does not assume a canonical hemodynamic response function.
source: In contrast to a standard convolution-based regression analysis, deconvolution does not assume a canonical hemodynamic response function.
evidence: This is a description of the deconvolution method.

claim: Deconvolution produces a better understanding of shape differences between individual hemodynamic response functions and achieves higher statistical power at both individual and group-levels.
source: This produces a better understanding of shape differences between individual hemodynamic response functions and achieves higher statistical power at both individual and group-levels (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the advantages of deconvolution, supported by citation.

claim: There might be differences in timing for the processing of concrete and abstract words.
source: Furthermore, there might be differences in timing for the processing of concrete and abstract words (Kroll and Merves, 1986).
evidence: This is a statement about potential timing differences, supported by citation.

claim: The 'concreteness effect' indicates that concrete words are processed faster and more accurately than abstract words.
source: In particular, the 'concreteness effect' indicates that concrete words are processed faster and more accurately than abstract words (Paivio et al., 1994; Jessen et al., 2000; Fliessbach et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about the concreteness effect, supported by citations.

claim: Amplitude modulation allows isolation of regions that exhibit activational fluctuations specifically in relation to the concreteness modulator beyond the 'main effect' and fluctuations in the amplitude response caused by other modulators.
source: In contrast, amplitude modulation allows us to isolate regions that exhibit activational fluctuations specifically in relation to the concreteness modulator beyond the 'main effect' and fluctuations in the amplitude response caused by other modulators included in our model.
evidence: This is a description of the advantage of amplitude modulation.

claim: The 20 amplitude-modulated beta-coefficients from the concrete-abstract contrasts were used in a linear mixed effects model for group-level analysis using '3dLME'.
source: We then used the 20 amplitude-modulated beta-coefficients from the concrete-abstract contrasts in a linear mixed effects model for group-level analysis using '3dLME' (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the group-level analysis method.

claim: To correct for multiple comparisons in the LME, a multi-threshold approach was used rather than choosing an arbitrary p value at the individual voxel level threshold.
source: To correct for multiple comparisons in the LME, we used a multi-threshold approach rather than choosing an arbitrary p value at the individual voxel level threshold.
evidence: This is a description of the multiple comparison correction method.

claim: A cluster simulation method was used to estimate the probability of noise-only clusters using the spatial autocorrelation function from the LME residuals.
source: In particular, we used a cluster simulation method to estimate the probability of noise-only clusters using the spatial autocorrelation function from the LME residuals ('3dFWHMx' and '3dClustSim').
evidence: This is a description of the cluster simulation method.

claim: The resulting coordinates of the center of mass of each cluster associated with modulation of concreteness and abstractness were inputed into Neurosynth.
source: The resulting coordinates of the center of mass of each cluster associated with modulation of concreteness and abstractness were inputed into Neurosynth (https://neurosynth.org/, Yarkoni et al., 2011), an online tool that includes activation maps of 14,371 neuroscientific studies (accessed April, 2023).
evidence: This is a description of the meta-analytic method.

claim: Neurosynth automatically mines all words in titles and abstracts of articles and performs a two-way ANOVA, testing for the presence of a non-zero association between terms reporting activation that overlaps with the input location.
source: Neurosynth automatically mines all words in titles and abstracts of these articles and performs a two-way ANOVA, testing for the presence of a non-zero association between terms reporting activation that overlaps with the input location.
evidence: This is a description of how Neurosynth works.

claim: The 'Peaks and Valleys Analysis' is a variant of the 'reverse correlation' method.
source: To provide more precise functional specificity, we used a variant of the 'reverse correlation' method (Hasson et al., 2004), called the 'Peaks and Valleys Analysis' (Hasson et al., 2008; Skipper et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a description of the peaks and valleys analysis method, supported by citations.

claim: The Peaks and Valleys Analysis assumes that if a brain region encodes certain features, then activity will rise (creating peaks) in that region when the feature is present in the stimulus and fall (resulting in valleys) when it is absent.
source: The approach assumes that, if a brain region encodes certain features, e.g. sensorimotor features, valence, or arousal, then activity will rise (creating peaks) in that region when the feature is present in the stimulus and fall (resulting in valleys) when it is absent.
evidence: This is a description of the assumption underlying the peaks and valleys analysis.

claim: The canonical model of the hemodynamic response function is said to peak at around 6 s after stimulus onset for stimuli of the length used in the study.
source: Given that the canonical model of the hemodynamic response function is said to peak at around 6 s after stimulus onset for stimuli of our length, we extracted the words that were mentioned at each peak and valley in a given cluster's time series with a 5- and 6 s lag (Figure 7, (2)).
evidence: This is a statement about the hemodynamic response function based on established knowledge.

claim: The Lancaster sensorimotor norms and norms for valence and arousal were used to determine a 13-dimensional experience-based representation for each word.
source: We then used the Lancaster sensorimotor norms (Lynott et al., 2020) and norms for valence and arousal (Warriner et al., 2013) to determine a 13-dimensional experience-based representation for each word (Figure 7, (3)), which included the dimensions: 'Auditory,' 'Gustatory,' 'Haptic,' 'Interoception,' 'Visual,' 'Hand_Arm,' 'Foot_Leg,' 'Torso,' 'Mouth,' 'Head,' 'Olfactory,' 'Valence,' and 'Arousal.'
evidence: This is a description of the norms used for the peaks and valleys analysis.

claim: To test predictions about contextual situatedness, a measure of contextual situatedness was estimated for each concrete and abstract word.
source: To test our predictions, we estimated a measure of contextual situatedness for each concrete and abstract word included in the first analysis.
evidence: This is a description of the method for estimating contextual situatedness.

claim: Two pre-trained visual recognition models, Faster R-CNN and OmniSource, were utilized to extract object features.
source: To that end, we utilized two pre-trained visual recognition models, Faster R-CNN (He et al., 2015) and OmniSource (Duan et al., 2020), to extract object features using computer vision toolboxes (Mkrtychian et al., 2019), respectively.
evidence: This is a description of the visual recognition models used, supported by citations.

claim: For each prediction frame, the object recognition model generated a list of detected object labels and kept those that had a prediction confidence of 90% or greater.
source: For each prediction frame (about every four frames, i.e. 4*0.04=0.16 s), the object recognition model generated a list of detected object labels and kept those that had a prediction confidence of 90% or greater (Figure 8, 1).
evidence: This is a description of the object recognition procedure.

claim: Objects that were recognized at least three standard deviations more often by the model compared to the mean recognition rate were excluded because they would bias the measure of situatedness.
source: Then, we excluded all objects that were recognized at least three standard deviations more often by the model compared to the mean recognition rate of objects (which was 682 appearances), because they would bias our measure of situatedness.
evidence: This is a description of the exclusion criteria for object labels.

claim: The excluded labels were 'person' (17,856 appearances per movie on average), 'chair' (9718 appearances per movie on average), and 'tie' (8123 appearances per movie on average).
source: These labels were 'person' (17,856 appearances per movie on average), 'chair' (9718 appearances per movie on average), and 'tie' (8123 appearances per movie on average).
evidence: This is a description of the excluded object labels.

claim: The final object features were represented as the average of the vectorized object labels using GloVe.
